query: Consider the following context: Temper embrittlement, characterized by a dramatic loss of ductility within a narrow temperature window, is ubiquitous in conventional alloys but is not reported in compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems. In that context, which material can be used for ductile–brittle–ductile transition, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Introducing an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy will exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition across a broad temperature window, primarily because its single-phase solid solution resists localized embrittling segregation and maintains ductile failure mechanisms even in temperature ranges where conventional alloys typically suffer temper embrittlement.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast, solutionized CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy with a single-phase, face-centered cubic structure and grain sizes in the micrometer range.
generation.intervention: Incrementally vary the testing temperature from cryogenic (e.g., −150 °C) to elevated temperatures (~600 °C) to capture any potential transition in mechanical behavior.
generation.conditions: Maintain a controlled atmosphere to prevent oxidation or surface embrittlement during heating, and ensure quasi-static tensile testing rates to capture the transition properly.
generation.structural_mediator: Suppressed segregation at grain boundaries and stable single-phase structure that reduces the formation of brittle precipitates or secondary phases responsible for embrittlement.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy and uniform element distribution reduce the driving force for phase separation and precipitation, minimizing embrittling grain-boundary effects and preserving ductile dislocation- and twinning-mediated deformation modes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional low-alloy steels, the CrMnFeCoNi alloy will retain higher overall ductility across the tested temperatures, exhibiting only a mild drop in ductility at intermediate temperatures and recovering ductility at higher temperatures, thereby showing a broadened ductile–brittle–ductile transition regime.
generation.baseline: Conventional low-alloy and medium-alloy steels often display severe temper embrittlement within a narrow range of temperatures, leading to abrupt ductility loss.
generation.boundary: Excessive introduction of secondary phases (e.g., via contaminated feedstock or improper alloy processing) may compromise single-phase stability and reduce ductility.
generation.uncertainty: Exact transition temperature ranges may vary with compositional variations, processing parameters, and microstructural features such as grain size; further systematic studies are required.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform tensile tests of cast and solutionized CrMnFeCoNi samples from −150 °C to 600 °C in controlled increments, tracking yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation-to-failure across this range.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy exhibits abrupt brittle failure at an intermediate temperature without showing any recovery of ductility at higher temperatures, the hypothesis is invalidated.
